title: Fontanelle Windows & Standard Views
front clue: Open fontanelles are acoustic doors: anterior for the survey, posterior and mastoid for the back
core concept: The anterior fontanelle is the primary window and stays open until roughly 9 to 18 months. A small-footprint sector or microconvex transducer of about 7.5 to 10 MHz is used, with a higher frequency for superficial structures. The standard survey is about six coronal planes, sweeping from the frontal horns through the third ventricle, the caudothalamic grooves, the bodies and trigones of the lateral ventricles, to the occipital lobes, plus five sagittal planes: a midline view showing the corpus callosum, cavum septi pellucidi, third and fourth ventricles and vermis, and parasagittal views of each lateral ventricle and the periventricular white matter. The posterior fontanelle improves views of the occipital horns, where blood layers dependently. The mastoid fontanelle, behind the ear, gives the best view of the posterior fossa: cerebellar hemispheres, fourth ventricle and cisterna magna. Normal choroid plexus is echogenic and lies in the bodies and trigones but never in the frontal or occipital horns.
why it matters: Exams test which window answers which question. Small intraventricular hemorrhage in the occipital horns and posterior fossa hemorrhage are both missed from the anterior fontanelle alone, so the posterior and mastoid views are not optional extras. A classic trap is calling normal choroid plexus in the trigone a clot; the clue is location, because choroid ends at the caudothalamic groove and is absent from the frontal and occipital horns. Another trap: the normal premature brain is smooth with few sulci, so a lissencephalic look at 26 weeks is expected rather than a malformation.
on the registry: Questions ask which fontanelle best shows the posterior fossa (mastoid) or occipital horn blood (posterior), and which midline structures belong on the sagittal view.
checkpoint: Anterior for the survey, posterior for the occipital horns, mastoid for the posterior fossa

title: Germinal Matrix Hemorrhage Grading
front clue: Fragile vessels at the caudothalamic groove bleed in tiny preterms: grade I to IV
core concept: The germinal matrix is a highly vascular, fragile layer beneath the ependyma, most prominent at the caudothalamic groove, that involutes by about 32 to 34 weeks. Infants born before 32 weeks or under 1500 g are at highest risk, and most bleeds occur within the first 72 hours of life. The Papile grading is the exam standard. Grade I is subependymal hemorrhage confined to the germinal matrix, seen as an echogenic focus at the caudothalamic groove. Grade II is intraventricular hemorrhage without ventricular dilation. Grade III is intraventricular hemorrhage filling and distending the ventricle. Grade IV, now usually termed periventricular hemorrhagic infarction, is parenchymal hemorrhage adjacent to the ventricle. Acute clot is echogenic; over weeks it retracts, becomes hypoechoic and centrally lucent, and a grade I bleed can evolve into a subependymal cyst while a parenchymal bleed evolves into a porencephalic cyst communicating with the ventricle. Screening is commonly performed at 7 to 14 days in very preterm infants and repeated later.
why it matters: Think of the grades as a story of spreading blood: matrix only, ventricle not dilated, ventricle dilated, then brain tissue. Grade III and IV carry the worst neurodevelopmental prognosis and the highest risk of post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus, so follow-up scans watch ventricular size. Traps include calling a bulky normal choroid plexus a grade II bleed, and forgetting that grade IV is a venous infarction rather than simple extension of grade III. A clot that has become hypoechoic is still a clot; echogenicity changes with age, not severity.
on the registry: Expect a description of an echogenic focus or ventricular blood with or without dilation and a request for the grade, or a question about the site of origin and peak timing.
checkpoint: Matrix, ventricle, dilated ventricle, parenchyma: I, II, III, IV

title: Periventricular Leukomalacia
front clue: Bright white matter beside the trigones that later turns into a cluster of holes
core concept: Periventricular leukomalacia is ischemic necrosis of the white matter in the vascular watershed of the premature brain, typically dorsal and lateral to the external angles of the lateral ventricles, near the trigones and beside the frontal horns. Early on it appears as increased periventricular echogenicity, which is significant when it is equal to or brighter than choroid plexus, is coarse or asymmetric, and persists beyond about 7 to 14 days. Transient normal flaring is homogeneous and less bright than choroid. In roughly 2 to 6 weeks the injured areas may cavitate into multiple small periventricular cysts that do not communicate with the ventricle. Later the cysts collapse and white matter volume loss produces ex vacuo ventriculomegaly with irregular ventricular margins. Risk factors include prematurity, hypotension, hypoxia-ischemia and maternal chorioamnionitis. The classic clinical outcome is spastic diplegia because the fibers to the legs pass closest to the ventricles.
why it matters: The key reasoning is time: echogenicity first, cysts weeks later, then volume loss. That is why a single early scan can miss PVL and why a late scan near term-equivalent age is part of screening. Separate PVL cysts, which sit in white matter and do not connect to the ventricle, from a porencephalic cyst after grade IV hemorrhage, which does. A common trap is labeling ex vacuo dilation as obstructive hydrocephalus; in PVL the head is not enlarging and the ventricles are irregular from tissue loss.
on the registry: Questions describe periventricular echogenicity brighter than choroid or cysts weeks after a hypotensive episode and ask for the diagnosis, the time to cavitation, or the expected motor outcome.
checkpoint: Bright, then cysts in 2 to 6 weeks, then volume loss and spastic diplegia

title: Hydrocephalus & Cerebral Doppler RI
front clue: Measure the ventricles, then let the resistive index tell you whether pressure is rising
core concept: Ventriculomegaly is enlargement of the ventricles; hydrocephalus implies increased CSF volume under pressure. In neonates the most common cause is post-hemorrhagic obstruction, followed by aqueductal stenosis, Chiari II malformation with myelomeningocele, and Dandy-Walker malformation. On coronal views the frontal horns lose their slit or comma shape and become rounded. Common measurements include the ventricular index (midline to lateral wall of the frontal horn, plotted against gestational age), anterior horn width (diagonal width greater than about 3 mm is enlarged), and the occipital horn or atrium. Dilation of the third and fourth ventricles helps locate the level of obstruction: lateral and third but normal fourth suggests aqueductal stenosis. Spectral Doppler of the anterior cerebral artery gives the resistive index, normally about 0.6 to 0.8 in term neonates. A rising RI, roughly above 0.8 to 0.9, or a marked increase with gentle fontanelle compression, suggests raised intracranial pressure. A low RI below about 0.5 to 0.6 suggests hyperemia and loss of autoregulation after asphyxia, or a high-flow intracranial arteriovenous shunt such as a vein of Galen malformation; by contrast, a patent ductus arteriosus lowers diastolic flow and raises the RI.
why it matters: Pattern the obstruction by which ventricles are dilated, then use Doppler as a physiologic tiebreaker when deciding whether dilation needs a shunt or reservoir. Rounded frontal horns signal pressure, while irregular ventricles with normal head growth suggest atrophy. Traps: RI is affected by a patent ductus arteriosus, heart rate and probe pressure, so compress the fontanelle gently and keep the infant calm. Also, a low RI is not reassuring; after hypoxic injury it can signal loss of autoregulation and a poor outcome.
on the registry: Expect questions on which ventricles dilate with aqueductal stenosis, normal neonatal RI ranges, and what high or low RI implies.
checkpoint: Round horns and a rising RI mean pressure; a low RI after asphyxia means trouble too
ai_review_status: fixed by AI review - please confirm
ai_review_note: corePiece (medium): A left-to-right shunt such as a patent ductus arteriosus steals diastolic flow and RAISES the cerebral RI (the card's own whyLock notes PDA effects); a low RI from shunting applies to an intracranial arteriovenous shunt such as vein of Galen malformation, so 'a shunt lesion' is misleading.

title: Dandy-Walker & Posterior Fossa Cysts
front clue: Big fourth ventricle cyst, missing vermis, tentorium pushed up
core concept: Dandy-Walker malformation is cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle that communicates with an enlarged posterior fossa, combined with hypoplasia or agenesis of the cerebellar vermis and elevation of the tentorium and torcula. The cerebellar hemispheres are splayed apart. Hydrocephalus is present in most cases, and associated anomalies such as agenesis of the corpus callosum and cardiac or chromosomal abnormalities are common. The midline sagittal and mastoid views are best for showing the vermis and the cyst. The differential matters. Mega cisterna magna is an enlarged cisterna magna, often defined as greater than 10 mm, with an intact vermis and normal fourth ventricle. Blake pouch cyst is a herniation of the fourth ventricle roof below an intact but upwardly rotated vermis. Arachnoid cyst is a separate CSF collection with mass effect that does not communicate with the fourth ventricle. In Chiari II malformation, by contrast, the posterior fossa is small and the cisterna magna is effaced.
why it matters: Reason by two questions: is the vermis present, and does the cyst connect with the fourth ventricle? Absent or small vermis plus communication equals Dandy-Walker. Intact vermis and normal fourth ventricle equals mega cisterna magna. A cyst displacing structures without communication equals arachnoid cyst. The classic trap is reading a big posterior fossa as Dandy-Walker without checking the vermis; the opposite trap is forgetting that Chiari II gives a small, crowded posterior fossa rather than a big one.
on the registry: Questions describe a posterior fossa cyst and ask you to separate Dandy-Walker from mega cisterna magna or arachnoid cyst based on the vermis and fourth ventricle.
checkpoint: Dandy-Walker: cyst plus fourth ventricle plus missing vermis plus high tentorium

title: Agenesis of the Corpus Callosum
front clue: No cavum, parallel ventricles, steer horns and sunray sulci
core concept: The corpus callosum is the large commissure connecting the hemispheres, seen on the midline sagittal view as a thin hypoechoic C-shaped band bordered by echogenic lines above the cavum septi pellucidi. In agenesis, complete or partial, the sagittal view shows absence of the band and gyri and sulci on the medial hemisphere radiating outward in a sunray or spoke-wheel pattern, with absence of the normal cingulate sulcus. Coronal views show absence of the cavum septi pellucidi, widely separated lateral ventricles whose frontal horns are narrow and pointed laterally in a steer horn or bull horn configuration, and a high-riding third ventricle that may extend between the hemispheres, sometimes forming an interhemispheric cyst. Axial or parasagittal views show parallel lateral ventricles with disproportionate enlargement of the occipital horns, called colpocephaly. Color Doppler may show an abnormal course of the pericallosal artery. Partial agenesis typically spares the anterior portion, the genu, because the callosum develops front to back except for the rostrum.
why it matters: Most exam items hinge on recognizing the cluster of indirect signs, because the absent structure itself is easy to overlook. If the cavum septi pellucidi is missing, ask why: callosal agenesis, septo-optic dysplasia and holoprosencephaly are the main answers. Do not confuse colpocephaly with hydrocephalus; the frontal horns in agenesis are narrow, not ballooned. Also remember the associations, including Dandy-Walker malformation, Chiari II, and syndromes such as Aicardi in girls.
on the registry: Expect a list of signs such as absent cavum, steer horn frontal horns and colpocephaly, with a request for the diagnosis.
checkpoint: Absent cavum plus colpocephaly plus sunray sulci equals callosal agenesis

title: Normal Pediatric Organ Sizes
front clue: Children are not small adults: every normal value scales with age
core concept: Pediatric normals change with age, so always compare measurements with age-based charts. The neonatal kidney measures about 4 to 5 cm, reaching about 6 cm by 1 year and adult range by adolescence; the two kidneys should be within about 1 cm of each other. The spleen upper limit is roughly 6 cm at 3 months, 7 cm at 1 year, 9 cm at 4 years, 10 cm at 8 years and 11 to 12 cm by 12 to 15 years. The common bile duct upper limit is about 1 mm in neonates, 2 mm in infants to 1 year, 4 mm in older children and about 7 mm in adolescents. The neonatal gallbladder is about 1.5 to 3 cm long after a fast. The neonatal pancreas is relatively large and may be iso- to hyperechoic. Prepubertal ovaries are about 1 cubic cm or less, and the infant adrenal gland is large, about one third of renal size at birth.
why it matters: The registry rarely expects you to memorize every chart value, but it does expect you to recognize which findings are normal for age and which are not. A 3 mm duct is normal in a teenager but dilated in a newborn. A 9 cm spleen is normal at 6 years but enlarged at 6 months. Asymmetry is often more telling than absolute size: a kidney more than about 1 cm smaller than its partner deserves explanation. Trap: the large neonatal adrenal is normal and should not be called a mass.
on the registry: Questions give a measurement and an age and ask whether it is normal, or ask for the typical neonatal renal length.
checkpoint: Neonatal kidney about 4 to 5 cm; neonatal duct about 1 mm; spleen grows about 1 cm every few years

title: Biliary Atresia
front clue: Jaundiced infant, tiny or absent gallbladder, echogenic cord above the portal vein
core concept: Biliary atresia is progressive inflammatory obliteration of the extrahepatic bile ducts, presenting with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, acholic stools and dark urine in the first weeks of life. It is the most common indication for pediatric liver transplant. Imaging is done after about a 4 hour fast. Key signs: the triangular cord sign, an echogenic triangular or tubular band of fibrous tissue anterior to the right portal vein bifurcation measuring about 4 mm or more in thickness; an absent or small gallbladder, generally under 1.5 cm long, or a gallbladder with an irregular, lobulated wall, the gallbladder ghost triad; failure of the gallbladder to contract after feeding; and an enlarged hepatic artery, about 1.5 mm or more, with subcapsular flow on color Doppler. Intrahepatic ducts are usually not dilated. Associations include the polysplenia or biliary atresia splenic malformation syndrome with heterotaxy, preduodenal portal vein, interrupted IVC with azygos continuation, and choledochal-like cysts in the cystic form. Hepatobiliary scintigraphy shows uptake without excretion to bowel.
why it matters: Timing drives prognosis. The Kasai portoenterostomy works best before about 60 days of age, so the sonographer is part of a race against time. The main differential is neonatal hepatitis, where the gallbladder is usually present and contracts. Trap one: a visible gallbladder does not exclude atresia; look at its size and wall. Trap two: expecting dilated ducts, which are classically absent because the ducts are obliterated rather than obstructed downstream. Always look at the spleen for polysplenia.
on the registry: Expect a jaundiced 4- to 6-week-old with an echogenic band anterior to the portal vein and a question naming the sign or the time-sensitive surgery.
checkpoint: Triangular cord 4 mm or more plus small, irregular gallbladder; Kasai before 60 days
ai_review_note: corePiece (low): The gallbladder ghost triad (Tan Kendrick) is gallbladder length under 1.9 cm, a thin or absent echogenic mucosal lining with an indistinct wall, and an irregular or lobular contour; the card ties the triad to a 1.5 cm cutoff and omits its components.

title: Choledochal Cyst
front clue: Cystic mass at the porta that connects to the bile duct, separate from the gallbladder
core concept: A choledochal cyst is a congenital cystic dilation of the bile ducts, more common in girls and in Asian populations, often linked to an anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction that allows pancreatic juice to reflux into the duct. The classic triad of pain, jaundice and a palpable right upper quadrant mass is present in only a minority. The Todani classification is tested: type I, fusiform or saccular dilation of the extrahepatic duct, is most common at about 80 to 90 percent; type II is a diverticulum of the extrahepatic duct; type III is a choledochocele bulging into the duodenum; type IV is multiple cysts, IVa intra- and extrahepatic and IVb extrahepatic only; type V is Caroli disease, multiple intrahepatic cysts. On ultrasound look for an anechoic cyst in the porta hepatis or pancreatic head that communicates directly with the common hepatic or bile duct, separate from the gallbladder, often with mild intrahepatic duct dilation. Sludge or stones can occur. Long-term risks include cholangitis, pancreatitis and cholangiocarcinoma.
why it matters: The core skill is proving communication with the duct, which separates a choledochal cyst from duplication cysts, hepatic cysts or pancreatic pseudocysts. In infants the crucial differential is cystic biliary atresia, which has a small cyst, a small or abnormal gallbladder and no intrahepatic dilation. In Caroli disease the central dot sign, a portal radicle surrounded by dilated ducts, is a classic clue. Surgical excision with hepaticojejunostomy is preferred because simple drainage leaves the malignant potential behind.
on the registry: Questions ask for the most common Todani type, the classic triad, or how to distinguish the cyst from the gallbladder and other right upper quadrant cysts.
checkpoint: Type I is the usual one; prove it connects to the duct

title: Hepatoblastoma & Pediatric Liver Masses
front clue: Under 3 with high AFP and a calcified solid liver mass: hepatoblastoma
core concept: Hepatoblastoma is the most common primary malignant liver tumor in children, usually occurring between 6 months and 3 years. It presents as an enlarging abdomen or mass with markedly elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein. Ultrasound shows a large, solid, often well-defined and heterogeneous mass, commonly in the right lobe, which may contain calcifications and septations; check the portal and hepatic veins and the IVC for invasion or tumor thrombus. Associations include Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, hemihypertrophy, familial adenomatous polyposis and extreme prematurity. Hepatocellular carcinoma occurs in older children and adolescents, often with underlying liver disease. The main benign mimic in young infants is infantile hepatic hemangioma, the most common benign hepatic vascular tumor, presenting before 6 months, with normal or only age-elevated AFP; it may be solitary or multifocal and highly vascular, can cause high-output heart failure and consumptive coagulopathy, and shows a large celiac axis with aortic caliber decreasing below it. Mesenchymal hamartoma is a multicystic benign mass in children under 2.
why it matters: Sort pediatric liver masses by age, AFP and vascularity. Infant under 6 months with heart failure and shunting suggests hemangioma. Toddler with very high AFP and calcified solid mass suggests hepatoblastoma. Teenager with cirrhosis or metabolic disease suggests hepatocellular carcinoma. Multicystic mass in a toddler suggests mesenchymal hamartoma. Trap: AFP is physiologically high in newborns, so it must be compared with age-adjusted values. Children with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome receive surveillance ultrasound for both hepatoblastoma and Wilms tumor.
on the registry: Expect a toddler with elevated AFP and a solid calcified liver mass, or an infant with high-output failure and a vascular mass, with a request for the likely diagnosis.
checkpoint: Hemangioma under 6 months, hepatoblastoma under 3 years with AFP, HCC in teens

title: Pediatric Spleen & Pancreas
front clue: Toddler with pancreatitis: think trauma first, including abuse
core concept: The pediatric spleen should be measured against age-based normals; causes of splenomegaly include infection such as mononucleosis, hemolytic anemias, portal hypertension, storage disease and leukemia or lymphoma. Accessory spleens, small round masses isoechoic to spleen near the hilum, are common normal variants. Asplenia and polysplenia occur with heterotaxy syndromes, and a wandering spleen on a long pedicle can torse. In sickle cell disease the spleen often autoinfarcts and becomes small and echogenic, while acute splenic sequestration causes rapid enlargement and anemia. The pediatric pancreas is relatively larger than in adults and can be iso- to hyperechoic compared with liver. In children, pancreatitis is most often caused by blunt trauma, including handlebar injury and non-accidental trauma, followed by drugs, infection, biliary disease, choledochal cyst and congenital anomalies such as pancreas divisum. Sonographic signs are enlargement, decreased echogenicity, peripancreatic fluid and pseudocyst. Cystic fibrosis causes a small, diffusely echogenic, fatty pancreas.
why it matters: Because children rarely have gallstone or alcohol pancreatitis, a young child with pancreatitis, a pseudocyst or a duodenal hematoma should raise concern for injury, including abuse, and findings must be documented carefully. Trap one: calling an accessory spleen a lymph node or mass; matching splenic echotexture is the tell. Trap two: assuming a bright pancreas is abnormal in a neonate. In heterotaxy, look for associated biliary atresia and cardiac anomalies.
on the registry: Questions ask for the most common cause of pediatric pancreatitis, the appearance of an accessory spleen, or the pancreatic appearance in cystic fibrosis.
checkpoint: Pediatric pancreatitis is trauma until proven otherwise; CF makes it small and bright
ai_review_note: whyLock (low): Registry texts still list trauma as the leading cause of pediatric pancreatitis, but contemporary series (e.g., INSPPIRE) show biliary or gallstone disease is common, especially in adolescents, so saying children 'rarely' have gallstone pancreatitis is outdated.

title: Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis
front clue: Projectile nonbilious vomiting at 2 to 8 weeks: 3 mm muscle, 15 mm channel
core concept: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis is idiopathic thickening of the pyloric muscle that obstructs gastric outflow. It typically presents between 2 and 12 weeks of age, peaking at 3 to 6 weeks, with projectile nonbilious vomiting, more often in first-born males, sometimes with a palpable olive and hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Scan with a high-frequency linear transducer with the infant supine or right side down, often after giving a little glucose water so fluid fills the antrum and pylorus. The standard diagnostic thresholds are a single muscle wall thickness of 3 mm or more and a pyloric channel length of 15 to 17 mm or more; a transverse pyloric diameter of about 13 mm or more supports the diagnosis. Signs include the target or doughnut sign in transverse, the cervix sign in longitudinal, the antral nipple sign of redundant mucosa protruding into the antrum, the shoulder sign, and failure of fluid to pass through the canal during several minutes of observation.
why it matters: Measure muscle only, from the outer edge of the hypoechoic muscle to the echogenic mucosa, and do not include mucosa in the wall thickness. Pylorospasm is the main trap: it can mimic stenosis briefly but the measurements fluctuate and fluid eventually passes, so watch over time. An overdistended stomach rotates the pylorus posteriorly; drain or reposition the infant. Bilious vomiting is not pyloric stenosis and should redirect you to malrotation with midgut volvulus. Treatment is pyloromyotomy.
on the registry: Expect measurement thresholds, the classic patient profile, and naming signs such as the cervix or antral nipple sign.
checkpoint: Three, fifteen: 3 mm muscle and 15 mm length mean stenosis

title: Intussusception
front clue: Toddler with colicky pain and a right-sided target over 2.5 cm
core concept: Intussusception is telescoping of a proximal bowel segment, the intussusceptum, into a distal segment, the intussuscipiens. The ileocolic type is most common, typically between 3 months and 3 years, peaking at about 6 months to 2 years, and is usually idiopathic, related to lymphoid hyperplasia in the terminal ileum. Classic findings are intermittent colicky pain with drawing up of the legs, vomiting, a palpable mass and currant jelly stool, though the full triad is uncommon. Ultrasound with a high-frequency linear probe is the first-line test. Look for a target or doughnut sign in transverse, often 3 to 5 cm in diameter and usually in the right upper quadrant near the hepatic flexure, and a pseudokidney or sandwich sign in longitudinal. Crescent-shaped mesenteric fat and lymph nodes are drawn into the mass. Transient small bowel to small bowel intussusceptions are smaller, generally under 2.5 cm, lack mesenteric fat, and often resolve spontaneously. Trapped fluid within the mass and absent color flow raise concern for ischemia and reduction failure.
why it matters: Ileocolic intussusception is treated by image-guided pneumatic or hydrostatic enema reduction unless there are contraindications: peritonitis, free air or shock. A pathologic lead point, such as Meckel diverticulum, duplication cyst, polyp or lymphoma, is more likely outside the typical age range, especially over about 5 years, so search for it. Trap: a small, peristalsing small bowel target in an otherwise well child is often transient and does not need enema reduction. Scan all four quadrants, because the mass can sit anywhere along the colon.
on the registry: Questions name the target or pseudokidney sign, ask the typical location and age, or ask which findings contraindicate enema reduction.
checkpoint: Ileocolic, right upper quadrant, over 2.5 cm; small and peristalsing is usually transient

title: Pediatric Appendicitis
front clue: Blind-ending, noncompressible tube over 6 mm, plus an appendicolith or hot fat
core concept: Appendicitis is the most common condition requiring emergency abdominal surgery in children. Ultrasound is the first-line imaging test, using graded compression with a high-frequency linear transducer to displace bowel gas, starting at the point of maximal tenderness and tracing the cecum to the appendix base. The inflamed appendix is a blind-ending, aperistaltic, noncompressible tubular structure with an outer diameter greater than 6 mm. Supporting findings include an echogenic shadowing appendicolith, echogenic inflamed periappendiceal fat, hyperemia of the wall on color Doppler, a target appearance in transverse, and adjacent free fluid or reactive nodes. Signs of perforation include loss of the echogenic submucosal layer, a periappendiceal fluid collection or abscess, complex free fluid and decreased wall flow. The appendix can be retrocecal or pelvic, so a full bladder or the left lateral decubitus position may help. In girls, consider ovarian torsion and cysts; in all children, consider mesenteric adenitis and terminal ileitis.
why it matters: The most useful single sign is a noncompressible diameter over 6 mm, but borderline diameters of 6 to 7 mm need secondary signs, especially inflamed fat. Perforation is common in young children because they present late, so the abscess may be the main finding. Traps include calling the terminal ileum the appendix, which is peristaltic and does not end blindly, and losing flow in a gangrenous appendix and mistaking that for normal. A nonvisualized appendix with no secondary signs makes appendicitis less likely but does not exclude it.
on the registry: Expect the diameter threshold, the role of graded compression, and signs of perforation.
checkpoint: Over 6 mm, noncompressible, blind-ending; inflamed fat seals the call

title: Malrotation & Midgut Volvulus
front clue: Bilious vomiting in a newborn: SMV right of SMA, or a whirlpool
core concept: Malrotation is abnormal rotation and fixation of the midgut during fetal development, leaving a narrow mesenteric base prone to twisting. Midgut volvulus, twisting of the bowel around the superior mesenteric artery, is a surgical emergency that threatens the entire midgut. Most cases present in the first month with bilious vomiting. On ultrasound, the superior mesenteric vein normally lies to the right of the superior mesenteric artery. In malrotation the SMV may lie directly anterior or to the left of the SMA, an inverted relationship. In volvulus, color Doppler shows the whirlpool sign: the SMV and mesentery wrapping clockwise around the SMA. Other clues include a dilated, fluid-filled proximal duodenum tapering to a beak, and failure to see the third portion of the duodenum crossing between the aorta and SMA in its normal retroperitoneal position. The upper GI series remains the reference test, showing an abnormally positioned duodenojejunal junction that fails to cross left of the spine at the level of the duodenal bulb.
why it matters: Bilious vomiting in an infant is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise, and delay can mean loss of the small bowel. A normal SMV and SMA relationship does not fully exclude malrotation, and an abnormal relationship can occur without it, so ultrasound adds to rather than replaces the upper GI series. Visualizing D3 crossing between the aorta and SMA is strong evidence of normal rotation. Trap: confusing bilious vomiting with pyloric stenosis, which is nonbilious. Treatment is the Ladd procedure.
on the registry: Questions test the normal SMA and SMV orientation, the whirlpool sign, and the urgency of bilious vomiting.
checkpoint: Vein right, artery left; a clockwise whirlpool means volvulus

title: Necrotizing Enterocolitis
front clue: Sick preemie with bright dots in the bowel wall and bubbles in the portal vein
core concept: Necrotizing enterocolitis is ischemic and inflammatory necrosis of the bowel, most common in premature, low-birth-weight infants within the first weeks of life, usually after feeds have started. It most often involves the terminal ileum and right colon. Clinical signs include feeding intolerance, abdominal distension, bloody stools and instability. Radiographs remain the first test, but ultrasound with a high-frequency linear transducer adds information about the bowel wall and perfusion. Findings include bowel wall thickening greater than about 2.5 to 3 mm or, more ominously, wall thinning under about 1 mm; pneumatosis intestinalis, seen as echogenic foci or a granular bright line within the wall; portal venous gas, seen as moving bright echoes in the portal vein and branching echogenic foci in the liver parenchyma; decreased or absent peristalsis; increased wall flow early and absent flow with necrosis; and free fluid. Complex free fluid with echoes or septations and focal fluid collections suggest perforation. Pneumoperitoneum can be seen as echogenic air anterior to the liver.
why it matters: Ultrasound is valued because it shows perfusion and fluid that radiographs cannot, and it can show deterioration before free air appears. Absent wall perfusion, thinning and complex fluid are the findings that push toward surgery. Trap: portal venous gas from umbilical venous catheter flushes can mimic NEC, so correlate clinically. Another trap is assuming normal wall thickness is reassuring; a thinned wall without flow is worse. Use gentle pressure, warmed gel and a fast exam on these fragile infants.
on the registry: Expect questions on the typical patient, the most common location, and the sonographic signs of pneumatosis, portal venous gas and perforation.
checkpoint: Preemie, terminal ileum, pneumatosis and portal gas; thin, flowless wall is bad

title: Enteric Duplication Cyst
front clue: A cyst with its own gut signature: bright mucosa inside, dark muscle outside
core concept: Enteric duplication cysts are congenital cystic or tubular structures that share a wall and blood supply with normal bowel. They can occur anywhere from the mouth to the anus but are most common in the ileum, followed by the esophagus and colon. Many are found prenatally or in early childhood; they may present with vomiting, pain, bleeding from ectopic gastric mucosa, obstruction, volvulus, or as a lead point for intussusception. The hallmark sonographic finding is the gut signature or double-wall sign: an inner echogenic mucosal layer and an outer hypoechoic muscular layer, sometimes with all five bowel wall layers visible. Peristalsis of the cyst wall may be seen in real time. Contents are usually anechoic but may contain debris or hemorrhage. The differential includes ovarian cyst in girls, choledochal cyst, mesenteric lymphatic malformation, which is thin-walled and often multiseptated, and Meckel diverticulum. Treatment is surgical excision.
why it matters: The gut signature is the answer to most exam questions on this topic, but beware the trap that any cyst with layered echogenic debris can mimic it; true layers are uniform and continuous around the cyst. A thick, layered wall excludes a simple mesenteric cyst. In an infant girl, an ovarian cyst with hemorrhage is a common mimic; finding both ovaries normal helps. Remember that duplication cysts can contain gastric mucosa, which explains bleeding and positive Meckel scans.
on the registry: Questions describe a cyst with an inner echogenic and outer hypoechoic wall and ask for the diagnosis or its most common location.
checkpoint: Double-wall gut signature equals duplication cyst; ileum is the usual home

title: Neonatal Kidney Appearance
front clue: Bright cortex and big dark pyramids are normal in a newborn
core concept: The neonatal kidney looks different from the adult kidney and these differences are frequently tested. Term neonatal kidneys measure about 4 to 5 cm. The renal cortex is often isoechoic or slightly hyperechoic compared with the liver and spleen, especially in premature infants, because of the higher density of glomeruli. The medullary pyramids are relatively large and hypoechoic, creating striking corticomedullary differentiation; they can be mistaken for dilated calyces or cysts. There is little renal sinus fat, so the central echo complex is small. Fetal lobulation, an undulating contour with indentations between lobes, is common and may persist. Transient medullary hyperechogenicity in the first days of life, often attributed to Tamm-Horsfall protein deposition, usually resolves. The adult pattern, with cortex hypoechoic to liver and less prominent pyramids, emerges over the first several months of life. Normal neonatal adrenal glands are large, with a hypoechoic cortex and echogenic central medulla, roughly one third the size of the kidney at birth.
why it matters: The trap is pathologizing normal anatomy. Prominent pyramids arranged around the sinus are not hydronephrosis; true calyceal dilation connects to the renal pelvis. Brightly echogenic cortex can be normal in a neonate but abnormal in an older child, where it suggests medical renal disease. Persistent medullary echogenicity beyond the first weeks suggests nephrocalcinosis, for example from furosemide therapy in premature infants. Postnatal scans for prenatal hydronephrosis are usually delayed beyond about 48 to 72 hours because early dehydration can hide dilation.
on the registry: Expect a question asking which neonatal renal feature is normal, such as hyperechoic cortex, prominent pyramids or fetal lobulation.
checkpoint: Newborn kidney: bright cortex, dark pyramids, little sinus fat, all normal

title: Hydronephrosis Grading & UPJ Obstruction
front clue: Big pelvis, dilated calyces, normal ureter and bladder: UPJ obstruction
core concept: The Society for Fetal Urology system grades hydronephrosis by the appearance of the pelvis, calyces and parenchyma. Grade 0 has no dilation. Grade 1 shows only a slightly visible renal pelvis. Grade 2 shows a dilated renal pelvis with a few calyces visible. Grade 3 shows dilation of the pelvis and all calyces with preserved parenchyma. Grade 4 adds parenchymal thinning. The newer urinary tract dilation, or UTD, classification uses the anteroposterior renal pelvic diameter, with about 10 mm or more abnormal postnatally, plus calyceal dilation, parenchymal thickness and appearance, ureters and bladder. Ureteropelvic junction obstruction is the most common cause of neonatal hydronephrosis. It is more common in boys and on the left and may be bilateral. Ultrasound shows a dilated renal pelvis and calyces that taper abruptly at the UPJ, with a normal-caliber ureter and normal bladder. Causes include intrinsic narrowing and crossing lower pole vessels. Diuretic renography, such as MAG3, assesses function and drainage. Contralateral anomalies are common.
why it matters: Locate the obstruction by following the dilation downstream. Dilated pelvis only implies UPJ; dilated ureter implies the UVJ, reflux or a ureterocele; a thick bladder and bilateral dilation in a boy implies posterior urethral valves. Measure the AP pelvic diameter in transverse at the hilum. Traps: scanning in the first 48 hours can underestimate dilation; an extrarenal pelvis can look dramatic without calyceal dilation; and reflux can mimic obstruction, which is why a VCUG is often paired with ultrasound.
on the registry: Questions describe the pelvis, calyces and parenchyma and ask for the SFU grade, or ask the most common cause of neonatal hydronephrosis.
checkpoint: SFU 3 is all calyces; SFU 4 adds thin cortex; UPJ spares the ureter

title: Posterior Urethral Valves
front clue: Boy with a thick bladder, bilateral hydro and a keyhole: valves
core concept: Posterior urethral valves are obstructing membranous folds in the posterior urethra and the most common cause of bladder outlet obstruction in male infants. They occur only in boys. Prenatally they may cause oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia. Postnatal ultrasound shows a thick-walled, trabeculated bladder, often distended or poorly emptying, with a dilated posterior urethra that, together with the bladder, creates the keyhole sign. Bilateral hydroureteronephrosis is typical, and the kidneys may be small, echogenic and contain cortical cysts, indicating renal dysplasia. Pressure pop-off mechanisms, such as a urinoma, perirenal fluid, urinary ascites or a large bladder diverticulum, may protect one kidney. The posterior urethra can be imaged by a transperineal approach during voiding. The voiding cystourethrogram is the diagnostic test, showing a dilated posterior urethra with an abrupt caliber change at the valve. Treatment is endoscopic valve ablation, but many boys develop chronic kidney disease.
why it matters: Reason from anatomy: an obstruction below the bladder dilates everything above it, so expect a thick bladder plus bilateral ureters and pelves. Unilateral dilation does not fit valves unless there is a pop-off or reflux into one side. Renal parenchymal echogenicity and cysts predict poorer renal outcome, so describe them. Trap: in a girl with similar findings, think of neurogenic bladder or urogenital sinus anomalies instead. Prune belly syndrome can mimic valves but usually has a large, smooth-walled bladder.
on the registry: Expect a male infant with a thick-walled bladder and bilateral hydronephrosis and a question naming the diagnosis, the keyhole sign or the confirmatory test.
checkpoint: Boys only: thick bladder, keyhole, bilateral hydro; VCUG confirms

title: Multicystic Dysplastic Kidney vs ARPKD
front clue: Grapes that do not connect, versus two huge bright kidneys
core concept: Multicystic dysplastic kidney is a nonfunctioning, dysplastic kidney replaced by multiple noncommunicating cysts of varying size with no normal renal parenchyma and no central renal pelvis. It is usually unilateral and found prenatally or as a neonatal flank mass. Nuclear medicine shows no function. The contralateral kidney has a high rate of anomalies, about 20 to 40 percent, especially vesicoureteral reflux and UPJ obstruction, and usually shows compensatory hypertrophy. Most MCDKs involute over time and are followed with ultrasound. Bilateral MCDK is lethal. Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease presents with bilaterally enlarged, diffusely echogenic kidneys with loss of corticomedullary differentiation, because innumerable tiny dilated collecting ducts, too small to resolve individually, create many interfaces. A thin hypoechoic peripheral rim of compressed cortex may be seen, and with high-frequency linear transducers small cysts of 1 to 2 mm may be visible. ARPKD is associated with congenital hepatic fibrosis and portal hypertension, inversely related to renal severity, and prenatal oligohydramnios with Potter sequence.
why it matters: For MCDK, the decisive question is whether the cysts communicate with a central pelvis. In severe hydronephrosis, dilated calyces connect to a medial pelvis; in MCDK, the largest cyst is usually not central and cysts do not connect. For ARPKD, reason about size: very large, bright kidneys in a neonate mean ARPKD, whereas autosomal dominant disease usually shows larger discrete cysts later in life. Always image the liver and spleen in ARPKD, and always scrutinize the contralateral kidney in MCDK.
on the registry: Questions ask how to separate MCDK from hydronephrosis, what to check in the opposite kidney, or which organ to evaluate with ARPKD.
checkpoint: MCDK: noncommunicating cysts, no function, check the other side; ARPKD: big bright pair plus liver fibrosis

title: Wilms Tumor
front clue: Preschooler with a big flank mass that grows from the kidney with a claw sign
core concept: Wilms tumor, or nephroblastoma, is the most common renal malignancy of childhood, with a peak at about 3 to 4 years. It usually presents as an asymptomatic, large flank or abdominal mass, sometimes with hematuria or hypertension. Sonographically it is a large, solid, well-circumscribed mass arising from the kidney, with heterogeneous echogenicity from hemorrhage, necrosis and cystic areas. The claw sign, renal parenchyma wrapping around the mass, confirms renal origin. Calcification is uncommon, seen in about 10 to 15 percent. Wilms tumor displaces adjacent vessels rather than encasing them, and it tends to invade the renal vein and IVC as tumor thrombus, which may extend into the right atrium; scan the renal vein, IVC and heart. Look also for the contralateral kidney, because about 5 to 10 percent are bilateral, and for liver metastases and lymph nodes. Associations include WAGR syndrome, Denys-Drash syndrome, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and hemihypertrophy, which warrant surveillance ultrasound, often every 3 months until about age 7 or 8. Nephroblastomatosis consists of precursor nephrogenic rests.
why it matters: The exam loves the Wilms versus neuroblastoma comparison. Wilms: older preschooler, arises from the kidney with a claw sign, rarely calcified, displaces vessels, invades veins, stays on one side of midline. Neuroblastoma: younger, suprarenal, frequently calcified, encases and lifts vessels, crosses midline. Trap: the neonate with a solid renal mass more likely has mesoblastic nephroma than Wilms. Avoid vigorous palpation, which could rupture the tumor; gentle scanning is the rule.
on the registry: Expect a large intrarenal mass in a 3-year-old with questions about the claw sign, venous extension or the difference from neuroblastoma.
checkpoint: Wilms: kidney, claw, displaces, invades veins, rarely calcifies

title: Neuroblastoma
front clue: Toddler with a calcified suprarenal mass that wraps around the aorta and crosses midline
core concept: Neuroblastoma is a malignant tumor of neural crest cells and the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood and the most common malignancy in infancy. Most children are under about 2 years at diagnosis, and nearly all under 5 or 6. The adrenal medulla is the most common origin, followed by paraspinal sympathetic ganglia in the abdomen, chest, neck and pelvis. Ultrasound shows a heterogeneous, poorly marginated solid suprarenal mass that displaces the kidney inferiorly and laterally without a claw sign. Calcifications are present in most cases, roughly 85 to 90 percent, and appear as echogenic foci with shadowing. The tumor characteristically encases and elevates vessels such as the aorta, IVC, celiac axis and SMA without invading their lumens, and it often crosses the midline. Urine catecholamine metabolites, vanillylmandelic acid and homovanillic acid, are elevated. Metastases go to bone, bone marrow, liver and skin; in infants under 18 months, stage MS (formerly 4S) disease may massively infiltrate the liver and often regresses. Periorbital bone metastases cause raccoon eyes.
why it matters: Reason by the vessel rule: neuroblastoma surrounds vessels, Wilms pushes them. Add age, calcification and origin and you can answer nearly every comparison question. Cystic neuroblastoma in a newborn can mimic adrenal hemorrhage; follow-up shows hemorrhage shrinking and losing echoes while tumor persists or grows, and tumor may show internal flow. Trap: forgetting to examine the liver, which can be diffusely infiltrated in infants rather than showing discrete nodules, so survey it fully.
on the registry: Questions test the calcification rate, vascular encasement, crossing of midline, catecholamine markers and stage MS liver involvement.
checkpoint: Neuroblastoma: adrenal, calcified, encases vessels, crosses midline, VMA and HVA up

title: Neonatal Adrenal Hemorrhage
front clue: Big baby after a hard delivery with a suprarenal mass that turns from bright to cystic
core concept: The neonatal adrenal gland is large and vascular, which makes it vulnerable to hemorrhage. Risk factors include birth trauma, large-for-gestational-age infants, infants of diabetic mothers, perinatal asphyxia, sepsis and coagulopathy. It occurs more often on the right, about 70 percent, and is bilateral in about 10 percent. Infants may present with a flank mass, anemia, prolonged jaundice or, rarely, adrenal insufficiency. The ultrasound appearance evolves with time. Acute hemorrhage is a solid-appearing, echogenic suprarenal mass. Over about 1 to 2 weeks it liquefies, becoming mixed and then hypoechoic or anechoic and cystic, and it shrinks progressively. Weeks to months later it may calcify, leaving a small echogenic, shadowing focus. A key feature is absence of internal blood flow on color Doppler. The left adrenal hemorrhage may be associated with left renal vein thrombosis because the left adrenal vein drains into the left renal vein; look for an enlarged kidney and thrombus. Management is conservative with serial ultrasound.
why it matters: Serial ultrasound is the diagnostic tool. Hemorrhage evolves and shrinks over days to weeks; neuroblastoma persists or grows and may show internal vascularity and elevated urine catecholamines. Reason from the timeline: a mass that was bright last week and is cystic and smaller this week is a resolving hemorrhage. Traps include calling an acute echogenic hemorrhage a solid tumor on a single scan, and forgetting to check the renal vein on the left side.
on the registry: Expect a neonate after a traumatic delivery with a suprarenal mass that changes over time and a question about its evolution or how to distinguish it from neuroblastoma.
checkpoint: Bright to cystic to smaller to calcified, with no flow: hemorrhage

title: Neonatal & Prepubertal Uterus and Ovaries
front clue: Hormones shape the uterus: bulbous at birth, tube-shaped in childhood, pear-shaped after puberty
core concept: Uterine shape changes with hormonal exposure. In the newborn, maternal and placental hormones stimulate the uterus, which measures about 3.5 cm long, and is prominent and often spade-shaped, with the cervix larger than or equal to the fundus, and a visible echogenic endometrial stripe, sometimes with a little fluid. Within a few months this stimulation fades. The prepubertal uterus is small, about 2.5 to 4 cm, tubular or spade-shaped, with the cervix equal to or larger than the fundus, a fundus to cervix ratio of about 1:1 or less, and a thin or invisible endometrium. After puberty, the fundus becomes larger than the cervix, with a ratio of about 2:1 to 3:1, and the uterus is pear-shaped. Ovaries are imaged through a full bladder. Prepubertal ovarian volume is usually about 1 cubic cm or less; small follicles are normal at all ages. Neonatal ovarian cysts are common, from maternal hormone stimulation. Cysts over about 2 cm are significant, and those over about 4 to 5 cm carry a risk of torsion.
why it matters: The exam asks you to match uterine morphology to hormonal status. An adult-shaped uterus or thick endometrium in a young child implies estrogen exposure, so consider precocious puberty or an estrogen-producing tumor. Ovarian volume above about 1 to 2 cubic cm in a young girl is also a puberty marker. Traps: calling small follicles pathologic, or forgetting that a large neonatal ovarian cyst may lie in the upper abdomen rather than the pelvis. A fluid-debris level in a neonatal cyst suggests hemorrhage or prior torsion.
on the registry: Questions give uterine dimensions or a fundus to cervix ratio and ask for the developmental stage, or ask the significance of a neonatal ovarian cyst.
checkpoint: Newborn bulbous, child tubular with cervix dominant, adult pear with fundus dominant

title: Ovarian Torsion
front clue: Big, swollen ovary with peripheral follicles: flow does not rule out torsion
core concept: Ovarian torsion is twisting of the ovary, often with the fallopian tube, on its vascular pedicle, compromising venous and lymphatic outflow and later arterial inflow. In children it can occur with a normal ovary because the adnexal ligaments are long and mobile, but lead points such as cysts and mature cystic teratoma are common. It is more frequent on the right. Patients present with acute, often intermittent pelvic or lower abdominal pain with nausea and vomiting. The most consistent sonographic finding is unilateral ovarian enlargement, markedly larger than the contralateral ovary, often several times its volume. The stroma becomes edematous and heterogeneous, and follicles are pushed to the periphery, the string of pearls appearance. The ovary may be displaced midline or above the uterus. Free fluid is common. The twisted pedicle may show a whirlpool sign. Doppler findings are variable: arterial and even venous flow may be preserved because of the dual ovarian and uterine arterial supply, so presence of flow does not exclude torsion.
why it matters: The registry trap is the flow trap. Asymmetric enlargement plus peripheral follicles in a child with pain should prompt urgent surgical consultation even if color Doppler shows flow. Compare volumes of both ovaries. Always look for a lead mass, such as a teratoma with an echogenic plug and shadowing. Right-sided torsion can mimic appendicitis, so the pelvis should be examined in girls with right lower quadrant pain. Detorsion saves the ovary even when it looks dark and congested at surgery.
on the registry: Expect a girl with acute pelvic pain and an enlarged ovary with peripheral follicles, and a question about the meaning of preserved Doppler flow.
checkpoint: Enlarged ovary plus peripheral follicles equals torsion, even with flow

title: Hydrometrocolpos
front clue: Midline cystic mass behind the bladder filled with echoes: a blocked vagina
core concept: Hydrocolpos is fluid distension of the vagina, and hydrometrocolpos is distension of both the vagina and uterus, caused by vaginal outflow obstruction. Causes include imperforate hymen, the most common, transverse vaginal septum, vaginal atresia, and more complex urogenital sinus or cloacal malformations. It presents in two peaks. In the neonate, maternal estrogen stimulates secretions that accumulate behind the obstruction, producing hydrometrocolpos and a lower abdominal mass. At menarche, menstrual blood accumulates, producing hematocolpos or hematometrocolpos with cyclic pain and primary amenorrhea. Ultrasound shows a midline, tubular or pear-shaped cystic mass posterior to the bladder and anterior to the rectum, often with low-level echoes or a fluid-debris level, with the small uterus perched on top or itself distended. The mass can compress the bladder and ureters, causing hydronephrosis. Transperineal imaging helps measure the thickness of the obstructing tissue. Associated renal and anorectal anomalies should be sought.
why it matters: Location is the key. A midline cystic mass between bladder and rectum in a girl is vaginal until proven otherwise; follow it up into the uterus to prove it. Separate it from ovarian cysts, which are lateral or upper abdominal and surrounded by ovarian tissue, and from anterior sacral meningocele or sacrococcygeal teratoma, which arise posterior to the rectum. Trap: in a newborn with a pelvic mass and a single perineal opening, think cloacal malformation and check the kidneys and spine.
on the registry: Questions describe a midline retrovesical cystic mass with echoes in a newborn or a girl at menarche and ask for the diagnosis or most common cause.
checkpoint: Imperforate hymen makes a retrovesical, echo-filled vagina at birth or menarche

title: Testicular Torsion
front clue: Teenager with sudden scrotal pain and a testis with no flow: the clock is ticking
core concept: Testicular torsion is twisting of the spermatic cord, cutting off venous outflow and then arterial inflow. It has two peaks. Neonatal extravaginal torsion occurs when the entire testis and tunica twist before fixation, often prenatally, and the testis is usually already infarcted. Intravaginal torsion, the more common form, occurs in adolescents, peaking around 12 to 18 years, due to the bell clapper deformity, in which the tunica vaginalis surrounds the testis completely and leaves it free to rotate. Presentation is sudden severe pain, nausea, a high-riding horizontal testis and absent cremasteric reflex. Ultrasound shows absent or markedly decreased intratesticular flow compared with the normal side. Early, the testis may look normal in grayscale; later it enlarges and becomes heterogeneous and hypoechoic, with a reactive hydrocele and scrotal wall thickening. The spermatic cord may show a whirlpool sign or a twisted, enlarged knot above the testis. Salvage is about 90 percent or more within 6 hours and falls sharply after 12 to 24 hours.
why it matters: Always compare with the asymptomatic side using identical settings, ideally in a side-by-side transverse view. Optimize for slow flow: low PRF and scale, low wall filter, high color gain, and power Doppler. Prepubertal testes have little flow normally, which makes comparison essential. Traps: partial torsion or spontaneous detorsion may show preserved or even increased flow, so the whirlpool cord is the deciding clue. Imaging must never delay surgery when clinical suspicion is high.
on the registry: Expect a teenager with acute pain and asymmetric flow, with questions about the bell clapper deformity, Doppler optimization or salvage timing.
checkpoint: Bell clapper, compare sides, slow-flow settings, salvage within 6 hours

title: Torsion of the Appendix Testis
front clue: Blue dot at the upper pole and a normal testicular flow: appendage torsion
core concept: The appendix testis is a small vestigial remnant of the Mullerian duct at the upper pole of the testis, near the epididymal head; the appendix epididymis is a remnant of the Wolffian duct. Torsion of one of these appendages is the most common cause of acute scrotal pain in prepubertal boys, peaking around 7 to 12 years. Pain is often more gradual and localized to the upper pole, and a small tender bluish nodule, the blue dot sign, may be seen through the skin. Ultrasound shows a round nodule adjacent to the upper pole of the testis or epididymal head, often greater than about 5 mm, which may be hyperechoic, hypoechoic or heterogeneous and shows no internal flow, with surrounding hyperemia of the epididymis and scrotal tissues, a reactive hydrocele and skin thickening. Intratesticular flow is normal. Management is conservative with analgesia. Epididymitis, the other main differential, shows an enlarged, hypoechoic, hyperemic epididymis; in prepubertal boys it should prompt a search for urinary tract anomalies.
why it matters: The decisive finding is normal flow in the testis itself. That changes management from emergency surgery to rest and analgesia. Peripheral hyperemia around the appendage can be misread as epididymitis, so look carefully at the upper pole for an avascular nodule. Trap: assuming increased flow always means infection; it may be a reactive response to appendage torsion or a detorsed testis. Age helps too: torsed appendages are typical before puberty, testicular torsion peaks in adolescence.
on the registry: Questions describe a prepubertal boy with upper pole pain, a blue dot and normal testicular flow, and ask for the diagnosis or management.
checkpoint: Avascular upper pole nodule with normal testicular flow: treat conservatively

title: Undescended Testis
front clue: Empty scrotum: look first in the inguinal canal, and remember small and dark
core concept: Cryptorchidism, failure of the testis to descend into the scrotum, affects about 3 percent of term boys and up to about 30 percent of premature boys, and spontaneous descent reduces this to about 1 percent by 1 year. It is more often unilateral and more common on the right. About 80 percent of undescended testes are palpable, and most lie in the inguinal canal or just beyond the external inguinal ring; others are intra-abdominal or ectopic. Ultrasound with a high-frequency linear probe searches from the scrotum through the inguinal canal to the internal ring. The undescended testis is typically smaller and slightly hypoechoic compared with the normal testis, oval, with a visible mediastinum testis, which helps separate it from a lymph node. A retractile testis can be manipulated into the scrotum and is normal. Complications include infertility, testicular malignancy, especially seminoma, with a risk several times higher, torsion and associated inguinal hernia. Orchiopexy is recommended by about 6 to 18 months.
why it matters: Ultrasound is good at finding inguinal testes but cannot reliably exclude an intra-abdominal testis, which is why current guidelines do not require routine ultrasound before referral and laparoscopy is used for nonpalpable testes. The mediastinum testis is the discriminator from lymph nodes. Trap: calling a small testis atrophic without comparing echotexture; another trap is missing bilateral nonpalpable testes in a newborn, which demands evaluation for disorders of sex development such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
on the registry: Expect the most common location, the appearance compared with a normal testis, or the long-term risks of cryptorchidism.
checkpoint: Inguinal canal is the usual home; small, hypoechoic, with a mediastinum testis

title: Hydrocele & Pediatric Scrotal Masses
front clue: Prepubertal testicular tumors are mostly teratoma or yolk sac; check AFP
core concept: A hydrocele is fluid between the layers of the tunica vaginalis, appearing as anechoic fluid surrounding the anterolateral testis. Congenital hydroceles are common in infants and usually resolve by 1 to 2 years. A communicating hydrocele connects with the peritoneum through a patent processus vaginalis, varies in size during the day and may accompany an indirect inguinal hernia, which appears as bowel with peristalsis or echogenic omentum in the inguinal canal or scrotum; incarceration shows fluid-filled, aperistaltic bowel with thickened wall. Reactive hydroceles accompany torsion, infection and trauma. Intratesticular masses in prepubertal boys differ from adults: mature teratoma and yolk sac tumor are the most common primary tumors, and yolk sac tumor raises alpha-fetoprotein. Epidermoid cyst shows an onion ring or target appearance without flow. Leukemia and lymphoma infiltration cause diffuse or focal hypoechoic, hypervascular enlargement, often bilateral, since the testis is a sanctuary site. Bilateral hypoechoic masses near the mediastinum in congenital adrenal hyperplasia are testicular adrenal rests.
why it matters: Separate extratesticular from intratesticular first: most extratesticular lesions are benign, most intratesticular solid masses need further workup. In prepubertal boys, many tumors are benign, so testis-sparing surgery may be considered. Traps: forgetting to scan the inguinal canal for a hernia when a hydrocele is large, and missing leukemic relapse because the enlarged testis was attributed to orchitis. Paratesticular rhabdomyosarcoma is an important extratesticular malignancy in children and adolescents, so a solid mass outside the testis is not automatically benign.
on the registry: Questions ask the most common prepubertal testicular tumors, the appearance of an epidermoid cyst, or why leukemia relapses in the testis.
checkpoint: Teratoma and yolk sac in little boys; AFP up with yolk sac; onion ring is epidermoid

title: Neonatal Spine Screening & Conus Level
front clue: Before the posterior arches ossify, the conus should end at or above L2-L3
core concept: The infant spine can be imaged sonographically until the posterior elements ossify, best in the first 3 months and usually possible until about 6 months. A high-frequency linear transducer is used with the infant prone or in a lateral decubitus position, often with a pillow under the abdomen to flex the spine. Indications include cutaneous stigmata above the gluteal crease such as a hair tuft, hemangioma, skin tag, subcutaneous mass, or a dimple larger than about 5 mm or more than about 2.5 cm from the anal verge, and anorectal malformations. The normal cord is hypoechoic with an echogenic central echo complex, tapering to the conus medullaris, which should lie at or above the L2-L3 disc space. A conus at L3 or below is abnormal. The filum terminale should be under about 2 mm thick, and cord and nerve roots should show normal pulsatile motion. Levels are counted from the last rib-bearing vertebra, T12, or upward from the lumbosacral junction.
why it matters: Level counting is the error-prone step. Use two methods, counting up from the sacrum and down from T12, and document with labeled images. A borderline conus at the L3 level, especially in a premature infant, may simply reflect immaturity and can be rescanned. Traps: a normal ventriculus terminalis, a small cystic dilation of the central canal at the conus, should not be called a syrinx, and a filar cyst is also a normal variant. Lack of cord motion is a functional sign of tethering.
on the registry: Expect the normal conus level, indications for screening, and the age window for spinal sonography.
checkpoint: Conus at or above L2-L3; filum under 2 mm; scan before 3 to 6 months
