title: Tethered Cord
front clue: Low-lying conus, fat in a thick filum, and a cord that does not move
core concept: Tethered cord syndrome occurs when the spinal cord is abnormally anchored caudally, preventing normal ascent and causing traction injury as the child grows. Causes include a thickened or fatty filum terminale, intradural lipoma, lipomyelomeningocele or lipomyelocele, diastematomyelia (split cord), dermal sinus tract and previous myelomeningocele repair. On ultrasound, findings include a conus at or below L3, a filum terminale thicker than about 2 mm, an echogenic filum from fat infiltration, an echogenic intradural lipoma in continuity with subcutaneous fat, a cord lying dorsally against the posterior canal, and reduced or absent pulsatile motion of the cord and nerve roots. A dermal sinus appears as a hypoechoic tract running from the skin toward the canal. Open defects such as myelomeningocele are usually obvious clinically and associated with Chiari II malformation and hydrocephalus. Clinically, tethering can cause bladder dysfunction, leg weakness, foot deformities, scoliosis and back pain. MRI confirms the anatomy before surgical untethering.
why it matters: The combination of position and motion is what matters. A low conus with absent pulsation is highly suggestive, while a borderline position with normal motion may simply be followed. Fat is echogenic, so a bright, thick filum is a reliable clue. Trap: closed defects under intact skin are easy to miss without stigmata, which is why cutaneous markers drive screening. Another trap is forgetting the association of myelomeningocele with Chiari II malformation, which links spine and brain imaging.
on the registry: Questions present a low conus or thick echogenic filum and ask for the diagnosis or its clinical consequences.
checkpoint: Low, thick, fatty and still: the tethered cord quartet

title: Graf Alpha Angle
front clue: Straight iliac line, bony roof: 60 degrees or more is a mature hip
core concept: The Graf method uses a static coronal image of the infant hip in lateral decubitus with a linear transducer. The standard plane must show a straight, horizontal iliac line parallel to the transducer, the lower limb of the ilium in the acetabular fossa, and the acetabular labrum. Three lines are drawn: the baseline, the bony roof line and the cartilaginous roof line. The alpha angle, between the baseline and the bony roof line, measures the depth of the bony acetabulum. The beta angle, between the baseline and the cartilaginous roof, measures cartilage coverage. Type I hips have an alpha angle of 60 degrees or more. Type IIa, 50 to 59 degrees, is physiologically immature under 3 months; type IIb is the same range after 3 months. Type IIc is 43 to 49 degrees with beta under 77, and type D has beta over 77, a decentering hip. Type III and IV are under 43 degrees and dislocated.
why it matters: Technique dominates: an oblique plane that does not show a straight iliac line gives a falsely low or high alpha angle, so the plane comes first, then the measurement. Timing matters because laxity is normal in the first weeks; screening of at-risk infants is typically performed around 4 to 6 weeks of age. Risk factors include breech presentation, female sex, family history, first-born status, oligohydramnios and tight swaddling. Trap: calling a type IIa hip under 3 months dysplastic rather than immature and due for follow-up.
on the registry: Expect alpha angle thresholds, the standard plane requirements, or the classification of a hip given its alpha angle and age.
checkpoint: Sixty or more is normal; fifty to fifty-nine is immature under 3 months

title: Femoral Head Coverage & Dynamic Hip Stress
front clue: At least half of the femoral head should sit under the bony acetabulum
core concept: Femoral head coverage, popularized by Harcke and Morin, is measured on the same coronal view used for Graf. Draw the iliac line and measure the portion of the femoral head diameter lying medial to it, beneath the bony acetabulum, as a percentage of the total diameter. Coverage of 50 percent or more is normal; roughly 40 to 50 percent is borderline or immature, especially in young infants; less than about 40 percent suggests subluxation, and very low coverage suggests dislocation. The dynamic examination uses a transverse flexion view with the hip flexed 90 degrees. In a normal hip the femoral head sits deep in the acetabulum between the pubis and ischium, forming a U shape. A gentle Barlow stress, adduction with posterior pressure, tests for posterior subluxation or dislocation, while the Ortolani maneuver relocates a dislocated hip. The femoral head is initially unossified, hypoechoic with speckled echoes; the ossific nucleus appears between about 2 and 8 months and eventually shadows the acetabulum, limiting ultrasound beyond about 6 months.
why it matters: Static coverage and dynamic stability answer complementary questions: Is the hip shallow, and is it unstable? Many immature hips stabilize by themselves, so serial imaging is common. Stress testing during Pavlik harness treatment is done only with physician direction, often without removing the harness. Trap: measuring coverage in an oblique plane exaggerates the result. After the ossific nucleus enlarges, radiographs replace ultrasound, typically after about 4 to 6 months of age.
on the registry: Questions ask for the normal coverage percentage, the meaning of a positive Barlow maneuver, or when ultrasound stops being useful.
checkpoint: Coverage 50 percent or more is normal; Barlow dislocates, Ortolani relocates

title: Hip Joint Effusion
front clue: Limping child: measure the anterior recess, but fluid alone cannot tell sepsis from synovitis
core concept: The hip joint effusion exam is an anterior approach with the child supine, the leg in neutral or slight external rotation, and a linear transducer placed parallel to the femoral neck. The anterior joint recess is measured from the anterior cortex of the femoral neck to the outer margin of the joint capsule. A distance greater than about 5 mm, or a difference of 2 mm or more compared with the asymptomatic side, indicates an effusion. Always scan both hips. Transient synovitis is the most common cause of acute hip pain and limp in children aged roughly 3 to 10 years, often after a viral illness, and resolves with rest. Septic arthritis is a surgical emergency that can destroy the joint; clinical predictors include fever over 38.5 degrees C, refusal to bear weight, elevated ESR and elevated white blood cell count. Ultrasound can guide aspiration of the joint for diagnosis. Other causes of limp include Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, slipped capital femoral epiphysis in adolescents, osteomyelitis and injury.
why it matters: The registry trap is believing that the appearance of fluid distinguishes septic arthritis from transient synovitis. Echogenic or anechoic, with or without synovial hyperemia, the fluid cannot reliably make that call; clinical criteria and aspiration do. A negative ultrasound with no effusion makes septic arthritis of the hip unlikely. Compare sides with the same technique and measure perpendicular to the femoral neck. Children with suspected osteomyelitis may show subperiosteal fluid next to the metaphysis.
on the registry: Expect the measurement threshold for effusion, the importance of comparison, and the inability of ultrasound to distinguish infection from synovitis.
checkpoint: Anterior recess over 5 mm or 2 mm more than the other side; aspirate to know

title: Pediatric Soft Tissue Masses
front clue: Lump in a child: cystic, vascular or solid, and how fast is it flowing?
core concept: Ultrasound is the first-line test for superficial pediatric masses. Infantile hemangioma is the most common tumor of infancy; it appears after birth, grows rapidly during a proliferative phase in the first months and involutes over years. In proliferation it is a well-defined solid mass with high vessel density, arterial and venous flow and low resistance, without arteriovenous shunting; involution brings increasing fat and decreasing flow. Vascular malformations are present at birth and grow with the child. Venous malformations are compressible hypoechoic channels with slow or no detectable flow and may contain echogenic shadowing phleboliths. Lymphatic malformations are multiloculated cystic masses with septations, fluid-fluid levels and no internal flow except in septa, common in the neck and axilla. Arteriovenous malformations show high-flow vessels without a soft tissue mass. Other common masses include lipomas, abscesses with peripheral hyperemia, foreign bodies, ganglion cysts and pilomatricoma, a calcified superficial nodule. Concern for malignancy, such as rhabdomyosarcoma, rises with size over about 5 cm, deep location, growth and chaotic vascularity.
why it matters: Organize by internal content and flow. Cystic with septations suggests a lymphatic malformation; compressible with phleboliths suggests a venous malformation; solid with dense flow in an infant suggests hemangioma; high-flow vessels without mass suggest AVM. The timeline matters: hemangiomas are not usually present at birth and then grow and fade, while malformations are present at birth and grow proportionally. Trap: calling an atypical solid, hypervascular mass in an older child a hemangioma; that needs MRI and possibly biopsy.
on the registry: Questions describe a soft tissue mass with specific flow and compressibility and ask for the likely lesion.
checkpoint: Hemangioma grows then fades; malformations grow with the child; lymphatics are cystic, veins compress

title: Fibromatosis Colli
front clue: Infant with torticollis and a fusiform, thickened sternocleidomastoid that moves with the muscle
core concept: Fibromatosis colli, also called pseudotumor of infancy, is benign fibrous thickening of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and a common cause of congenital muscular torticollis. It presents at about 2 to 8 weeks of age with a firm neck mass and head tilt toward the affected side, with the chin turned away. Risk factors include birth trauma, breech presentation, forceps delivery and primiparity, and it can be associated with developmental dysplasia of the hip. Ultrasound with a high-frequency linear transducer shows fusiform enlargement of the sternocleidomastoid, usually in the lower two thirds, with variable echogenicity, isoechoic, hyperechoic or heterogeneous, and preserved muscle fibers. The mass moves with the muscle and is contained within it, with no separate discrete lesion, no adjacent lymphadenopathy, no fluid collection and no calcification. Comparison with the contralateral normal muscle is essential, in both longitudinal and transverse planes. Treatment is physical therapy with stretching, and most cases resolve within months; a few require surgical release.
why it matters: The diagnosis rests on proving that the mass is the muscle itself. If the lesion lies outside the sternocleidomastoid or displaces it, think of lymph nodes, branchial cleft cysts, lymphatic malformation or neuroblastoma instead. The correct answer is almost never biopsy, because the history and imaging are characteristic. Trap: calling the enlarged muscle a mass because of heterogeneous echogenicity. Because of shared risk factors, these infants are often screened for hip dysplasia.
on the registry: Expect a 4-week-old with torticollis and a neck mass and questions on the involved muscle, the appearance and the treatment.
checkpoint: Fusiform SCM in a torticollis infant: compare sides, stretch it, do not biopsy

title: Thyroglossal Duct & Branchial Cleft Cysts
front clue: Midline and moves with the tongue, or lateral at the angle of the jaw
core concept: Thyroglossal duct cyst is the most common congenital neck mass in children. It forms along the path of thyroid descent from the foramen cecum to the lower neck and typically lies in the midline or just off midline, near the hyoid bone, often embedded in the infrahyoid strap muscles. It classically moves upward with swallowing or tongue protrusion. On ultrasound it may be anechoic with posterior enhancement but is often pseudosolid, with internal echoes from proteinaceous fluid or infection. Before surgical removal by the Sistrunk procedure, which includes the central hyoid, confirm a normal thyroid gland in its usual location, because ectopic thyroid tissue may be the only functioning thyroid. Branchial cleft cysts arise from incomplete obliteration of the branchial apparatus. The second branchial cleft cyst accounts for about 90 to 95 percent and lies at the angle of the mandible, anteromedial to the sternocleidomastoid, posterior to the submandibular gland and lateral to the carotid vessels. It is usually anechoic with thin walls but can become complex when infected.
why it matters: Location is the most powerful discriminator: midline means thyroglossal, lateral at the mandibular angle means second branchial cleft. Both may look solid because of debris, so look for posterior enhancement and absence of internal flow. The most tested pearl is to document the normal thyroid before thyroglossal cyst excision. Trap: a solid component with flow within a thyroglossal cyst in an older child raises concern for papillary thyroid carcinoma arising in the cyst.
on the registry: Questions describe the location and mobility of a neck cyst and ask for the diagnosis or the key structure to document before surgery.
checkpoint: Midline plus tongue motion is thyroglossal; check the thyroid bed first

title: Cervical Lymphadenopathy
front clue: Oval with a bright hilum is reactive; round, hilum-less and chaotic flow worries you
core concept: Cervical lymph nodes are very common in children and most are reactive to viral or bacterial infection. A normal or reactive node is oval, with a long to short axis ratio greater than about 2, a hypoechoic cortex, an echogenic fatty hilum and hilar vascularity on color Doppler. A short-axis diameter over about 1 cm is generally considered enlarged, though larger reactive nodes are common in the upper neck. Suppurative lymphadenitis, often from Staphylococcus aureus or group A streptococcus, produces an enlarged tender node that may liquefy into an abscess with central hypoechoic or anechoic fluid, no internal flow, peripheral hyperemia and surrounding echogenic inflamed fat; ultrasound identifies drainable collections and guides aspiration. Atypical mycobacterial infection causes matted nodes with necrosis and overlying skin involvement. Kawasaki disease may present with unilateral cervical adenopathy. Features suggesting malignancy, such as lymphoma or metastatic disease, include round shape, loss of the echogenic hilum, very hypoechoic or heterogeneous cortex, peripheral or chaotic vascularity, matting and supraclavicular location.
why it matters: The exam wants you to separate benign, infected and suspicious nodes by morphology. Shape and hilum come first, then vascular pattern, then the clinical picture. The major practical role of ultrasound is detecting a liquefied, drainable abscess versus phlegmon, since that changes management. Trap: a supraclavicular node in a child is always concerning, even if it looks fairly normal. Another trap is calling a partly cystic branchial cleft cyst an abscessed node without recognizing its typical location.
on the registry: Expect questions on features of a reactive node versus a malignant one, and the appearance of a suppurative node that needs drainage.
checkpoint: Oval plus hilum plus hilar flow is reassuring; round and hilum-less is not

title: Normal Thymus
front clue: A soft, starry-sky organ in the infant chest that drapes around vessels without pushing them
core concept: The thymus is a lymphoid organ in the anterior superior mediastinum that is relatively large in infants and young children and involutes after puberty. On chest radiographs it can mimic a mass or cardiomegaly, producing the sail sign, so ultrasound is often used to confirm that a widened mediastinum is normal thymus. It is imaged through suprasternal, parasternal and sometimes subxiphoid windows with a linear or small curvilinear transducer. The normal thymus is homogeneous, with echogenicity similar to or slightly less than liver or spleen, and contains fine echogenic linear strands and dots that create a starry-sky appearance. It is soft and pliable; it changes shape with respiration and conforms to adjacent structures, draping around the great vessels and heart without compressing or displacing them. Normal flow is present without mass effect. The thymus shrinks rapidly with stress, illness or steroids and may rebound afterward. Ectopic cervical thymus can appear as a neck mass with the same echotexture and continuity with the mediastinal thymus.
why it matters: The goal is to recognize normal tissue and avoid unnecessary CT. Normal thymus has a consistent echotexture, molds to vessels, and never compresses the airway or vessels. Features that should raise concern for an anterior mediastinal mass, such as lymphoma or a germ cell tumor, include heterogeneous echotexture, calcification, cystic components, displacement of vessels or airway, and a lobulated contour. Trap: assuming a small thymus in a sick infant is abnormal; it is often stress involution.
on the registry: Questions ask for the normal thymic echotexture or features that distinguish normal thymus from a mediastinal mass.
checkpoint: Starry sky, soft, molds around vessels; never compresses

title: Pediatric Pleural Effusion
front clue: Fluid above the diaphragm: septations mean a complicated effusion that may need drainage
core concept: Ultrasound is ideal for pleural assessment in children because it is portable, radiation-free and better than radiographs at characterizing fluid. Scan from below the costal margin or through intercostal spaces with the child sitting, supine or decubitus, using a curved or linear transducer. A pleural effusion is fluid between the visceral and parietal pleura above the diaphragm. Normally the spine is not seen above the diaphragm because aerated lung blocks it; with an effusion or consolidation the spine is visible above the diaphragm, the spine sign. Simple effusions are anechoic, but anechoic fluid can be either transudate or exudate. Echogenic fluid, swirling particles, septations, loculations and pleural thickening indicate an exudate and suggest a complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema. Consolidated lung appears hepatized, tissue-like, with dynamic air bronchograms that move with respiration, separating pneumonia from atelectasis. Ultrasound guides thoracentesis and chest tube placement and identifies septations that may favor fibrinolytic therapy or thoracoscopic surgery.
why it matters: Characterize, then quantify. Septations and loculations change management because simple drainage may fail. The key trap is assuming anechoic fluid is a transudate; many early exudates are anechoic. Another trap is mistaking consolidated lung or the spleen for fluid. In neonates, chylothorax is a common cause of isolated effusion, and in older children, parapneumonic effusion dominates. Always image the opposite side and the pericardium, and document fluid depth so serial exams can be compared.
on the registry: Questions ask what septations indicate, the meaning of the spine sign, or how ultrasound guides drainage.
checkpoint: Anechoic can be anything; septations mean complicated; spine sign means fluid or consolidation

title: Pediatric Tumor Overview
front clue: Match the tumor to the organ and the age: a map of pediatric malignancy
core concept: Leukemia is the most common childhood cancer overall, followed by central nervous system tumors. Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor and the most common malignancy of infancy. Organizing tumors by location and age helps on the exam. Kidney: Wilms tumor peaks at 3 to 4 years; mesoblastic nephroma is the most common solid renal mass in the neonate; renal cell carcinoma appears in adolescents. Adrenal: neuroblastoma. Liver: infantile hemangioma under 6 months, hepatoblastoma in children under 3, hepatocellular carcinoma in teens. Pelvis: rhabdomyosarcoma of the bladder, prostate or vagina, the grape-like sarcoma botryoides; sacrococcygeal teratoma, the most common neonatal tumor, arising from the coccyx with cystic and solid components. Ovary: germ cell tumors dominate, with mature cystic teratoma the most common ovarian neoplasm in children, showing an echogenic Rokitansky nodule and shadowing. Testis: teratoma and yolk sac tumor before puberty. Mediastinum and nodes: lymphoma. Soft tissue: rhabdomyosarcoma. Tumor markers include AFP for hepatoblastoma and yolk sac tumor and urine catecholamines for neuroblastoma.
why it matters: Many exam questions can be answered with only the age, organ and marker. A neonate with a solid renal mass has mesoblastic nephroma, not Wilms. A 2-year-old with a calcified adrenal mass and high catecholamines has neuroblastoma. A girl with abdominal pain and a calcified adnexal mass with an echogenic plug has a teratoma. Trap: forgetting that physiologic AFP is very high in newborns. Remember also that ultrasound documents organ of origin, vascular involvement and metastases, especially to the liver.
on the registry: Expect questions asking the most common tumor for a given organ and age, or the marker associated with a tumor.
checkpoint: Organ plus age plus marker usually names the tumor

title: Pediatric Preparation & Sedation
front clue: Short fasts, warm gel, and sedation only rarely for ultrasound
core concept: Preparation is tailored to age and exam. For gallbladder and biliary imaging, a fast of about 3 to 4 hours is typical in infants and about 4 to 6 hours in older children, balanced against hypoglycemia risk; biliary atresia studies usually use about 4 hours. Pyloric exams need no fasting, and a feed of clear fluid can help. Pelvic exams require a full bladder by drinking fluids or, rarely, by catheter in a child who cannot cooperate. Neonatal intensive care exams are done at the bedside, often through incubator portholes, with warmed gel, minimal exposure, strict hand hygiene and transducer disinfection, and attention to lines, leads and monitors. Sedation is rarely needed for ultrasound because it is painless and can be paused. When sedation is used, for example for Doppler or long procedures, it requires a physician order, fasting according to institutional guidelines, continuous monitoring including pulse oximetry, trained staff and resuscitation equipment.
why it matters: Fasting reasons matter: a contracted gallbladder after feeding can mimic wall thickening or an absent gallbladder in suspected biliary atresia, but over-fasting a neonate is unsafe. Thermoregulation is a major risk in premature infants, so keep them covered and warm. Infection control is essential in the NICU because these infants are immunocompromised. Trap: offering sedation as a default rather than using distraction, feeding and patience. If sedation is used, the sonographer must recognize respiratory depression and know who to call.
on the registry: Questions ask appropriate fasting for a biliary exam, preparation for a pelvic study, or monitoring needed during sedation.
checkpoint: Fast short, warm the gel, guard the temperature, and sedate only with monitoring

title: Child-Friendly Technique & Transducer Selection
front clue: Small patient, high frequency: linear for surface, small curved for depth
core concept: Children have less body fat and smaller dimensions, so higher frequencies can be used for better resolution. A high-frequency linear transducer, about 9 to 18 MHz, is the workhorse for the pylorus, appendix and bowel, intussusception, scrotum, hips, spine, neck, soft tissues and the superficial liver in infants. A small-footprint curved or microconvex transducer of about 5 to 9 MHz suits the infant and child abdomen and pelvis, and a low-frequency curved array is used in larger adolescents. A sector or microconvex probe fits the fontanelles and intercostal spaces. Technique is age-appropriate: let a parent stay, explain what will happen in simple words, warm the gel, use toys, videos, songs or bubbles for distraction, and give infants a bottle or pacifier. Use a child life specialist when available. Start with the least threatening area and the most important images first, because cooperation may be brief. Keep imaging pressure gentle, especially over a painful abdomen, and adjust depth, focus and gain to the small field of view.
why it matters: The principle is that resolution and cooperation both drive diagnostic quality. A crying child creates bowel gas, motion and an abdomen too tense to compress, so investing in comfort saves time. Know the order of priorities so that the critical images are captured early. Traps include using a large adult curved probe on a neonate, which wastes resolution, and forgetting that frequency must drop in obese adolescents. Never restrain a child forcefully; involve parents and staff and follow institutional policies.
on the registry: Expect questions on choosing a transducer for a given pediatric exam and on age-appropriate communication and distraction.
checkpoint: Linear high frequency for small or superficial targets; get the critical images first

title: Non-Accidental Trauma Awareness
front clue: Injuries that do not fit the story: document objectively and report per policy
core concept: Non-accidental trauma, or child abuse, should be considered when injuries are inconsistent with the history or the child's developmental stage, when injuries of different ages are present, or when care was delayed. Infants and young children are most at risk. Abdominal injuries are a leading cause of death in abused children and include liver and splenic lacerations, duodenal hematoma, pancreatic injury with pancreatitis or pseudocyst, and bowel perforation, particularly in toddlers without a clear mechanism. Cranial sonography can detect extra-axial fluid or parenchymal injury in infants with an open fontanelle, but CT and MRI are needed for head trauma, and ultrasound does not exclude intracranial injury. Skeletal surveys remain the standard for fractures; ultrasound may show cortical disruption or periosteal reaction. The sonographer's role is to document findings objectively with labeled images and measurements, avoid accusatory comments, preserve privacy, and communicate concerns to the interpreting physician. Healthcare workers are mandated reporters in all US states and must follow institutional reporting policies.
why it matters: The registry tests awareness and professional behavior more than diagnosis. Patterns raise suspicion: duodenal hematoma or pancreatitis in a toddler, injuries of different ages, and history that changes. The trap is acting outside scope, such as confronting caregivers or discussing suspicions with the family. Document carefully, include both sides, and report through the proper channel. Another trap is assuming a normal head ultrasound excludes inflicted injury; it does not, and CT or MRI is required.
on the registry: Expect scenario questions on the sonographer's correct action when abuse is suspected and on abdominal injuries that suggest it.
checkpoint: Document, do not accuse, and report through policy

title: ALARA in Children
front clue: No ionizing radiation, but still as low as reasonably achievable: watch TI, MI and Doppler time
core concept: Ultrasound is preferred in children because it uses no ionizing radiation, but it deposits energy and the ALARA principle, as low as reasonably achievable, still applies. Two on-screen indices guide safety. The thermal index estimates potential temperature rise: TIS for soft tissue, TIB when bone lies at or near the focus, as in the fetal or neonatal skull and spine, and TIC when bone is at the skin surface. The mechanical index estimates the potential for cavitation and nonthermal effects and is most relevant where gas is present, such as lung and bowel. Spectral and color Doppler generally produce higher intensities and higher TI than grayscale, so keep Doppler time short, especially in the neonatal head and over ossifying bone. Practical steps include starting with a low output power and increasing receiver gain before increasing output, minimizing dwell time, using freeze when not actively scanning, choosing appropriate presets for pediatric and neonatal exams, and avoiding nondiagnostic or entertainment scanning. Exam time should match clinical need.
why it matters: Remember that gain amplifies received signals without increasing patient exposure, while output power increases exposure, so gain is the first adjustment when images are dark. Thermal effects increase with dwell time, bone absorption and Doppler, and infants have limited ability to dissipate heat. Trap: assuming no radiation means no risk. Another trap is choosing TIS for a scan where bone lies at the focus. Pediatric presets reduce default output and are an easy safety habit.
on the registry: Questions ask which index applies to a given situation, which control to adjust first, or which modes raise exposure.
checkpoint: Raise gain before power, shorten Doppler, and pick the right TI for the tissue
